modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-airstream-: Phonation driven by compressing air in the cheeks and oral cavity; the tongue or lips may vibrate. It commonly occurs in short imitative sounds and tongue-out sounds, and can also support brief stretches of speech.
Use ↀ to mark stretches produced with a buccal airstream. In continuous transcription, write {ↀ … ↀ}.
This marks the source of airstream power. Buccal, pulmonic egressive, pulmonic ingressive, and oesophageal airstreams are recorded separately.

Speech produced during inhalation, with air flowing from the mouth and nose toward the lungs. Inhaled exclamations and continuous counting with alternating exhalation and inhalation can use this airstream.
↓ may follow an individual phonetic symbol; {↓ … ↓} can mark a complete stretch of ingressive speech.
Pulmonic ingression differs from the laryngeal airstream mechanism of implosives. This downward arrow also does not indicate falling tone.

Oesophageal speech introduces air into the oesophagus and then releases it, vibrating tissue at the pharyngo-oesophageal junction to provide an alternative to the glottal source. The oral cavity, tongue, and lips continue to articulate.
Use Œ or braces labelled Œ to show the scope of oesophageal airflow. Œ comes from the initial OE of oesophageal.
Air stored in the oesophagus supplies the power. Tracheo-oesophageal speech instead directs exhaled pulmonic air into the oesophagus. Capital Œ here has a different function from the vowel œ.
Exhaled pulmonic air enters the oesophagus through a passage between the trachea and oesophagus, driving vibration at the pharyngo-oesophageal junction before supralaryngeal articulation.
Use Ю for tracheo-oesophageal speech; a continuous stretch can be written {Ю … Ю}.
It can use an alternative sound source similar to oesophageal speech, but its driving airflow comes from the lungs and can sustain longer stretches of phonation.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-phonation-: A phonation type common in everyday speech and singing, producing sound through relatively regular periodic vocal-fold vibration. In VoQS, V is one of four basic phonation labels alongside F, W, and C, and underlies several compound phonation types.
Use V for modal voice; write {V … V} when a continuous stretch needs to be delimited.
The pitch range of modal voice varies between speakers. Modal names a phonation type; other phonation types can also occur in healthy, natural speech.

The vocal folds lengthen longitudinally, their vibrating edges become thinner, and less tissue participates in vibration, usually producing a higher, lighter sound. Falsetto may be leaky and may combine with whispery, creaky, or harsh qualities.
F marks falsetto. A dot below, a tilde below, and an exclamation mark further indicate whispery, creaky, and harsh qualities respectively.

Falsetto and modal voice can overlap in pitch; distinguish them using phonatory configuration and auditory quality together. Falsetto uses the vocal folds; the false vocal folds involved in ventricular phonation are a separate concept.

Airflow through a narrowed laryngeal passage produces turbulence noise without sustained periodic vocal-fold vibration. Typical whisper includes laryngeal constriction, with the anterior glottis approximated and a posterior opening, potentially resembling a Y shape.
Use W for whisper. Voiceless consonants within a whispered stretch retain their individual phonetic transcriptions; the label summarizes the stretch's phonatory setting.
Whisper W primarily uses airflow noise as its sound source. Whispery voice Ṿ retains the whisper setting with vocal-fold vibration added. Whisper can also be relatively loud.

Slow, distinguishable vocal-fold pulses are prominent, sounding like a series of small crackles or taps. Vibration is commonly low in frequency with little airflow; pulse spacing may be regular or irregular.
C is one of VoQS's basic phonation labels and denotes creak. Add an exclamation mark for harsh creak C!.
VoQS lists creak C separately from creaky voice V̰, the latter indicating voicing with creaky qualities. Their realizations can be similar; use a consistent transcription standard.

Vocal-fold vibration is added to the laryngeal setting of whisper, combining voiced energy with appreciable airflow-friction noise. Laryngeal constriction and the posterior airflow passage jointly shape this voice quality.
A single dot below V marks whispery voice; use {Ṿ … Ṿ} for a continuous stretch.

Unlike whisper W, whispery voice includes vocal-fold vibration. Compared with breathy voice V̤, its larynx is usually more constricted and its turbulence more prominent. A single dot below and two dots below are distinct marks.

Voicing has creaky pulses, potentially including low-frequency vibration, multiple pulses, or irregular vibration, often heard as grainy or intermittent. Creaky voice may have different vibratory patterns across speakers and contexts.
A tilde below V indicates creaky voice. C separately labels creak as a basic type, whereas V̰ labels voicing with creaky qualities.

Low pitch is common, but fundamental frequency alone does not characterize every kind of creaky voice. Creaky and harsh qualities can combine, marked separately by a tilde below and an exclamation mark.

Considerable airflow escapes during vocal-fold vibration, mixing a breath-like airflow sound with periodic sound. A typical setting has less complete glottal closure and a relatively open supralaryngeal passage.
Two dots below V mark breathy voice. For an individual segment, the breathy-voice diacritic can instead be placed below the corresponding IPA letter.

Breathy V̤ and whispery Ṿ voice both include vocal-fold vibration. Breathy voice usually has a more open laryngeal setting; whispery voice has whisper-like constriction. Two dots below do not denote a separate following aspirated segment.

Phonation with marked harshness, often involving laryngeal constriction, irregular vibration, and increased noise. Aryepiglottic and ventricular constriction may contribute; low-pitched harsh voice may also involve aryepiglottic-fold vibration.
Add ! after V for harsh voice; {V! … V!} marks its scope. 1, 2, and 3 may mark relative harshness from weaker to stronger.

Harsh voice can occur at low, middle, or high pitch. The exclamation mark denotes harshness; record loudness separately. Use ventricular phonation V‼ when ventricular-fold vibration needs explicit identification.
A compound phonation type combining falsetto with whispery qualities. Falsetto vocal-fold vibration co-occurs with whisper-like laryngeal constriction and airflow-friction noise.
F denotes falsetto and a dot below denotes whispery quality; together they form F̣.
It differs from whispery voice Ṿ in using a falsetto setting. Simple air leakage in falsetto can be breathy and should be distinguished from the whispery quality marked here.
Falsetto with creaky qualities, adding a pulsed or irregular auditory character to the lighter falsetto sound. VoQS lists it as a compound phonation type.
F denotes falsetto and the tilde below denotes creaky quality, giving F̰.
This label records both qualities within the same stretch. If creak is simply followed by falsetto, mark two separate successive stretches.
Falsetto with harsh qualities, containing appreciable noise or irregular vibration.
Add ! after F for the combination of falsetto and harsh qualities, F!.
F specifies the basic falsetto setting and ! adds harshness. Use this label for high-pitched sounds only when both features are present.
More pronounced harshness is added to creak's slow-pulsed phonation. The basic creak type is retained while harsh qualities are also recorded.
C denotes creak and ! denotes harshness; together they form C!.
C! and harsh creaky voice V̰! retain the distinction between C and V̰. Apply the same criteria used for separate creak and creaky-voice labels.
Voiced whisper-like phonation also has a harsh quality. Vocal-fold vibration, whisper-like airflow noise, and harshness combine in the same stretch.
The dot below V denotes whispery quality and the following ! denotes harshness: Ṿ!.
Compared with whispery voice Ṿ, it adds harshness. Compared with harsh voice V!, it explicitly retains whispery quality.
Voicing combines creaky pulses and harshness, heard as both creaky graininess and harsh roughness.
The tilde below V denotes creak and ! denotes harshness, giving V̰!.
Creakiness and harshness are recorded separately. If only one is present, use V̰ or V! as appropriate.
Voicing combines whisper-like airflow noise with creaky pulses, producing whispery creaky voice.
Retain both a tilde below and a dot below V, denoting creaky and whispery qualities respectively.
It adds creakiness to whispery voice Ṿ and whisperiness to creaky voice V̰. Both diacritics contribute to the meaning.
Whispery creaky voice with additional harshness, combining voicing, whisper-like noise, creaky pulses, and harsh qualities.
V is the base; a tilde below denotes creak, a dot below denotes whisperiness, and ! denotes harshness.
Compared with whispery creaky voice V̰̣, this label additionally marks harshness. Every component should correspond to an actual feature in the transcribed stretch.
Falsetto is the basic setting, combined with whisper-like noise and creaky pulses. The label brings falsetto, whisperiness, and creakiness together.
A tilde below and a dot below F mark whispery creaky falsetto.
Compared with whispery creaky voice V̰̣, the base changes to falsetto F. The qualities combine over the same stretch; use the same complete label at both boundaries.
Whispery creaky falsetto with additional harshness, combining falsetto, whispery, creaky, and harsh qualities.
F supplies the falsetto base; a tilde below, a dot below, and ! add creaky, whispery, and harsh qualities respectively.
It adds harshness to whispery creaky falsetto F̰̣. Select the complete combination according to the features heard and observed.
A relatively relaxed phonatory setting, potentially with less laryngeal squeezing. Lax and tense describe tension relative to a reference setting and may involve different laryngeal adjustments.
The weak-articulation diacritic below V marks lax voice. Use a consistent reference when judging it.
Lax voice contrasts with tense voice V͈. Loudness, air leakage, and tension can vary independently; clear breathy or whispery qualities may be recorded separately.

A relatively tense, pressed, or effortful phonatory setting, often involving stronger vocal-fold adduction and laryngeal constriction. Tense voice summarizes the phonatory presentation; the specific constriction site may be described further.
The strong-articulation diacritic below V marks pressed or tense voice.
Tense voice contrasts with lax voice V͉. Tension and roughness are different observational dimensions; clear creaky or harsh qualities can be recorded separately.

The ventricular folds are also called the false vocal folds, hence false-vocal-fold phonation. Located above the vocal folds, they vibrate in the airflow and contribute to the sound source; the vocal folds below may vibrate simultaneously.
The double exclamation mark ‼ after V marks ventricular phonation. Use {V‼ … V‼} for a sustained stretch.
Ventricular phonation explicitly involves ventricular-fold vibration. Harsh voice V! summarizes roughness, whereas falsetto F uses a falsetto pattern of vocal-fold vibration.

Also called double-pitched voice, with two pitch components heard simultaneously. Joint vocal-fold and ventricular-fold vibration can produce it; vocal-fold asymmetry or complex vibratory patterns may also produce a similar quality.
Add the voicing diacritic below the ventricular-phonation label V‼ to form V̬‼.

Diplophonia emphasizes two simultaneously perceived pitches. General roughness and a percept in which the fundamental and an enhanced overtone are both prominent require separate assessment in the actual material.

Ventricular-fold vibration contributes to phonation together with whispery quality; also called whispery false-vocal-fold phonation. The sound combines a ventricular source and whisper-like airflow noise.
A dot below V‼ combines whispery quality with ventricular phonation.
It adds whisperiness to ventricular phonation V‼ and explicitly identifies ventricular-fold vibration compared with whispery voice Ṿ.

The aryepiglottic folds vibrate in the airflow and contribute to the sound source. These tissues are at the laryngeal inlet; their vibration can combine with vocal-fold phonation and may contribute to low-pitched harsh voice.
Superscript small-capital AA after V marks the aryepiglottic folds as a vibrating source.
The ventricular folds and aryepiglottic folds are different structures, marked by V‼ and this label respectively. Specific vibratory sources require laryngeal observation.

Records irregular voice-quality fluctuations or phonatory breaks associated with spasmodic dysphonia. The symbol depicts alternation or fluctuation and may summarize changes across a stretch of speech.
It can stand alone or combine with other voice-quality labels to delimit changes. Adductor/abductor type and the presence of tremor can be added as text annotations.
This symbol does not distinguish disorder subtypes, and a single voice-quality fluctuation cannot establish a diagnosis. Record known circumstances and actual observations.
An electrolarynx provides vibration as the sound source, which is articulated into speech by the oral cavity, tongue, and lips. Users can start and stop the device to support voicing contrasts.
И indicates that an electrolarynx serves as the source. A scope label may encompass the relevant stretch of speech.

The stretch can still contain voiceless sounds and pauses; the device need not vibrate continuously throughout it. Oesophageal and tracheo-oesophageal speech instead use human tissue as an alternative sound source.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-larynx-001: The larynx occupies a relatively high position during speech, changing vocal-tract length and resonance. L denotes the larynx, and the raising diacritic below indicates upward displacement.
L̝ marks a raised larynx and can delimit a stretch jointly with a phonation-type label.
Larynx height and vocal-fold vibration frequency are recorded separately. A raised larynx may accompany pitch changes, but high pitch alone does not establish larynx position.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-larynx-002: The larynx occupies a relatively low position during speech, lengthening the vocal tract and changing resonance. L denotes the larynx, and the lowering diacritic below indicates downward displacement.
L̞ marks a lowered larynx, judged against the same speaker's reference position.
A lowered larynx can combine with different pitches and phonation types. Low pitch and a relaxed auditory quality alone cannot replace observation of larynx position.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-labial-001: The lips sustain a relatively open rounded posture, narrowing horizontally while retaining a sizeable vertical opening. The lip shape of the vowel œ offers a reference.
Superscript oe after V denotes an open-rounded setting. Degree numbers or a sustained scope can be added.
The lip opening is larger than in close rounding Vʷ. The label summarizes sustained lip posture; individual segments retain their actual phonetic transcriptions.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-labial-002: The lips remain rounded and protruded with a small aperture, comparable to the lip posture of the vowel u.
Superscript w after V denotes a close-rounded setting.
This VoQS label describes lip posture. If velarization is also present, record it separately with the velarized-voice label.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-labial-003: The lips remain spread toward the sides over a stretch of speech, widening the mouth horizontally.
V͍ summarizes a spread-lip setting. Mark degree and scope when needed.
Lip spreading emphasizes horizontal widening, while open jaw J̞ emphasizes lowering of the mandible. The two movements can be observed and recorded separately.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-labial-004: The lower lip remains close to the upper teeth during a stretch of speech, producing a prominent labiodental setting or secondary articulation.
The labiodentalization diacritic after V marks this sustained voice quality.
The label summarizes the stretch's labiodental setting. Individual labiodental consonants still use their corresponding IPA symbols, such as f and v.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-lingual-00: The tongue tip has a prominent articulatory role across a stretch of speech, with coronal sounds tending toward apical configurations.
The apical diacritic below V denotes an overall apicalized setting.
Apicalization emphasizes the active part of the tongue; dentalization and alveolarization emphasize the passive place approached.
The tongue blade, immediately behind the tip, plays a prominent role across a stretch of speech, with coronal sounds tending toward laminal configurations.
The laminal diacritic below V denotes a laminalized setting.
It differs from apicalization V̺ in the tongue part primarily involved. Laminalization alone does not specify a unique passive place of articulation.
Speech persistently exhibits a retroflex configuration and quality. The tongue tip curls upward and backward, affecting the resonance of neighbouring segments and the stretch as a whole.
Use V˞ for a retroflex setting. Treat retroflexion or rhoticity of individual segments according to the relevant transcription conventions.
The relationship between retroflex settings and different r sounds varies across languages and speakers; rhotic quality can arise from different tongue shapes.
Coronal articulation persistently approaches the upper-teeth region, producing a prominent dentalized setting.
A dental diacritic below V marks the stretch affected by dentalization.
Dentalization and alveolarization V͇ differ in passive place of articulation; involvement of the tip or blade can be recorded separately.
Coronal articulation persistently approaches the alveolar ridge. Parallel to dentalization, the label emphasizes an overall articulatory tendency toward the alveolar region.
A double horizontal line below V denotes an alveolarized setting.
Dentalization V̪ approaches the upper teeth; alveolarization V͇ approaches the alveolar ridge. Individual segments retain their places in segmental transcription.
Speech sustains a palato-alveolar configuration: the tongue's coronal region articulates near the area behind the alveolar ridge while the tongue body rises toward the hard palate.
Retain both the double horizontal line below V and superscript j to mark a palato-alveolarized setting.
When comparing with alveolarization V͇ or palatalization Vʲ alone, consider both coronal and tongue-body configurations.
The tongue body stays raised toward the hard palate, giving a stretch of speech widespread secondary palatal articulation. The primary articulations of individual segments may remain.
Vʲ marks the scope of palatalization; degree numbers can further distinguish its strength.
A palatalized setting can overlay segments at several places of articulation without requiring all of them to be transcribed as palatals.
The back of the tongue remains raised or approximated toward the soft palate, adding secondary articulation and resonance changes in the velar region across a stretch of speech.
Superscript ˠ after V marks a velarized setting.
Distinguish it from uvularization Vʶ by the region approached. Velarization describes tongue configuration; nasalization controlled by velum raising or lowering is recorded separately.
The back of the tongue remains approximated toward the uvula and surrounding area, adding secondary uvular articulation to speech.
Superscript small-capital R after V denotes a uvularized setting.
Uvular constriction is usually farther back than velar constriction. A sustained setting is treated separately from the segmental transcription of a single uvular consonant.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-lingual-01: A stretch of speech has a quality associated with pharyngeal narrowing. Tongue-root retraction and laryngeal-inlet constriction may jointly contribute, changing resonance in the lower vocal tract.
The pharyngealization diacritic ˤ after V marks a pharyngealized setting.

Pharyngeal, tongue-root, and laryngeal movements can be related. In comparison with laryngopharyngealization V̙ˤ, note the latter's additional specification of tongue-root retraction and laryngopharyngeal constriction.
Tongue-root retraction combines with laryngopharyngeal constriction to create a prominent laryngopharyngealized setting. Both tongue-root retraction and pharyngealization remain in the symbol.
Add the retracted-tongue-root diacritic below V and pharyngealization ˤ to form V̙ˤ.
Compared with pharyngealization Vˤ, this label explicitly marks tongue-root retraction. The component gestures may be coupled; consider the overall configuration when transcribing.
An overall configuration involving the faucial pillars and adjacent pharynx, potentially with a lowered larynx and longitudinal pharyngeal expansion, producing a hollow, yawn-like quality.
Superscript H with a bar after V marks faucalization; the shape evokes two pillars and their connection to indicate the faucial region.

Local tension or approximation of the faucial pillars can coexist with overall pharyngeal expansion. This setting can also occur at relatively high pitch; distinguish it from pharyngealization Vˤ and lowered larynx L̞ alone.
The velopharyngeal passage is open, allowing nasal resonance and a sustained nasalized quality across speech.
A nasalization diacritic above V denotes nasalized voice. Nasalization of an individual segment can be marked directly on its IPA letter.
A sustained nasalized setting and an individual nasal consonant are recorded separately. Nasal resonance and audible nasal airflow noise are also distinct observations.
Nasal resonance is reduced, weakening the nasal component of sounds expected to be nasal or nasalized.
The denasalization diacritic above V marks a denasalized setting across a stretch of speech.
Compare with the language's and speaker's reference setting. Partial denasalization of an individual nasal can use the corresponding extIPA diacritic.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-jaw-001.de: The mandible remains relatively low and open, enlarging the oral aperture; vowels may tend toward more open qualities overall.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-jaw-001.us: J denotes the jaw and the lowering diacritic denotes an open-jaw position, giving J̞.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-jaw-001.co: Jaw position and tongue height influence each other but can also be adjusted separately. Transcribe each vowel's actual quality individually.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-jaw-002.de: The mandible remains relatively high and closed, reducing the oral aperture; vowels may tend toward closer qualities overall.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-jaw-002.us: J with the raising diacritic denotes a close-jaw position: J̝.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-jaw-002.co: It contrasts with open jaw J̞. The label records a sustained jaw position; transcribe individual vowel height and actual aperture from observation.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-jaw-003.de: The mandible remains displaced toward the speaker's own right over a stretch of speech, producing a lateralized mouth posture and articulatory setting.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-jaw-003.us: A rightward-displacement diacritic below J denotes jaw displacement to the right.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-jaw-003.co: Left and right are referenced to the speaker. When facing the speaker, visually observed left and right are reversed relative to the label.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-jaw-004.de: The mandible remains displaced toward the speaker's own left over a stretch of speech, producing a lateralized mouth posture and articulatory setting.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-jaw-004.us: A leftward-displacement diacritic below J denotes jaw displacement to the left.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-jaw-004.co: Left and right are referenced to the speaker. This is symmetrical with rightward jaw displacement J͔; protrusion and degree of opening can be recorded separately.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-jaw-005.de: The mandible protrudes relative to the maxilla, shifting the lower teeth and lip and affecting articulation and resonance across speech.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-jaw-005.us: The advancement diacritic below J denotes jaw protrusion.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-jaw-005.co: The label describes jaw posture during speech. Dental occlusion and whether the tongue extends outside the mouth require separate observation; Θ can mark tongue protrusion.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-jaw-006.de: The tongue remains protruded outside the mouth across a stretch of speech, with at least the tip extended; stronger protrusion may visibly expose the blade too.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-jaw-006.us: Capital Θ summarizes a tongue-protrusion setting. Degree numbers may indicate relative extent.
modules.ipa-plus.content.voqs-jaw-006.co: Lowercase θ transcribes a dental fricative; Θ marks a sustained voice-quality setting. An individual interdental segment and tongue protrusion across a stretch are recorded separately.
Placed beside a voice-quality label, it indicates a relatively weak quality; for example, 1V! denotes weak harsh voice.
Click to insert 1. A continuous stretch may be written {1V! … 1V!}, with matching labels at both ends.
1, 2, and 3 denote relatively weak, moderate, and strong degrees. Use a consistent reference; these do not correspond to fixed acoustic values.
Placed beside a voice-quality label, it indicates a moderate degree; for example, 2V! denotes moderately harsh voice.
Click to insert 2 and combine it with applicable voice-quality labels in scope markers.
Degree is judged for the marked quality. Harshness, loudness, and pitch are recorded separately.
Placed beside a voice-quality label, it indicates a relatively strong quality; for example, 3V! denotes strong harsh voice.
Click to insert 3; use matching degrees and voice-quality labels at both ends of a scope.
The numbers indicate relative degree in transcription and do not directly provide pathological severity or a clinical-scale score.
Starts the scope of a voice quality. Place the quality label after the opening brace, followed by the affected segments.
Click to insert {. For example, {V! starts a harsh-voice span, closed by V!}.
Braces delimit voice quality. Square brackets used for segmental transcription follow IPA conventions separately.
Ends the scope of a voice quality. Repeat the corresponding quality label before the closing brace to match the opening.
Click to insert }. For example, a complete harsh-voice span is {V! … V!}.
Voice-quality labels and degrees must match at both ends. Close multiple labels in their nesting order.
Provides a pair of empty braces for a continuous voice-quality span. Add matching labels and the segments inside.
Wraps selected text; without a selection, places the cursor between the braces. Complete it using {label … label}.
The ellipsis only indicates where content goes. The empty-scope button actually inserts a pair of braces.
Two V! labels delimit a harsh-voice stretch, beginning after the left label and ending before the right label.
Wraps selected text; without a selection, places the cursor between the labels. Add matching degree numbers at both ends if needed.
The template shows the scope of the voice quality. Speech outside the span retains its original transcription and is unaffected by these labels.
The very harsh voice stretch from the original chart's example. The 3V! labels at both ends mark strong harshness throughout the stretch.
Click to insert the complete example stretch, including degree, labels, braces, and segmental transcription.
3 modifies the degree of harshness; ˈ before a word still marks stress. Voice-quality labels, segments, and stress transcription carry different information.
The original chart's full example successively shows modal voice, strong harsh voice, then a raised larynx with weak harsh voice. Its final stretch combines L̝ and 1V!, illustrating joint marking of larynx position and phonatory quality.
The button shows a compact preview. Clicking inserts the complete example with square brackets, stress, and two labelled stretches.
Labels from different dimensions can combine within a voice-quality span and close in reverse order at the end. Each degree number modifies only its corresponding quality.
